q: Comparable company analysis (trading comps) is what category of valuation method?
explain: Comps value a company relative to how similar public companies are priced, unlike a DCF, which is an intrinsic method.

sources.title: Comparable Company Analysis - Complete Guide
sources.quote: Comps is a relative form of valuation, unlike a discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis, which is an intrinsic form of valuation .

sources.title: Comparable Company Analysis | Trading Comps Tutorial
sources.quote: Comparable Company Analysis is a relative valuation method in which a company’s value is derived from comparisons to the current stock prices of similar companies in the market.

q: Which premium is embedded in precedent transaction multiples but not in trading comps multiples?
explain: Precedents look at prices paid to acquire companies, so the multiples include the premium paid to gain control; comps reflect current public trading prices.
hook: Buying the whole company costs extra for the steering wheel.

sources.title: Precedent Transaction Analysis - Definition, Steps
sources.quote: However, “comps” are current multiples that can be observed in the public markets, while “precedents” include a takeover premium that took place in the past.

sources.title: Precedent Transactions Analysis - Examples, Templates | Macabacus
sources.quote: The purpose is similar to that of comparable companies analysis, except that examining prior acquisitions can give a sense of the premium paid to gain control of the target (the “control premium”).

q: Because of the control premium, which are generally higher: transaction multiples or trading multiples?
wrong: Neither; it depends only on leverage
explain: Acquirers pay a control premium over the unaffected price, so precedent transaction multiples are generally higher than trading multiples.
hook: Control costs more than a single share.

sources.title: Precedent Transactions Analysis - Examples, Templates | Macabacus
sources.quote: Because of the control premium, transaction multiples are generally higher than trading multiples.

sources.title: Precedent Transaction Analysis | Transaction Comps Tutorial
sources.quote: Transaction comps analysis typically yields the highest valuation because it looks at valuations for companies that were acquired – meaning that a control premium is included in the offer price.

q: Control premium (%) equals the offer price per share divided by which share price, minus 1?
explain: The control premium is what the acquirer pays over the unaffected market trading price, i.e. the price before the deal news affected it.
hook: Premium over the price the deal hasn't touched yet.

sources.title: Precedent Transaction Analysis | Transaction Comps Tutorial
sources.quote: A control premium is defined as the amount that an acquirer paid over the unaffected market trading share price of the company being acquired, typically expressed as a percentage. Control Premium (%) = (Offer Price Per Share ÷ “Unaffected” Stock Price) – 1

q: What is the adjustment of a company's financial data to align with the calendar year-end (December 31) called?
explain: Calendarization standardizes peers with different fiscal year-ends so their multiples cover the same period and are truly comparable.
hook: Calendar-ize: line everyone up on the same calendar.

sources.title: Calendarization | Financial Definition + Example
sources.quote: Calendarization is the adjustment of a company’s financial data and operating performance to align with the calendar year-end date, i.e. December 31.

sources.title: Calendarization - Overview, Formula, How it Works
sources.quote: However, calendarization adjusts the fiscal year to the fiscal year of the parent or valuing company so that there is a “clean” basis for comparison.

q: In the calendarization formula, what value of 'Month' is used for a company whose fiscal year ends June 30?
explain: 'Month' is the month in which the fiscal year ends; June is month six, so half the calendar year comes from the fiscal year actual and half from the next fiscal year.

sources.title: Calendarization | Financial Definition + Example
sources.quote: Here, the term "Month" refers to the month the company's fiscal year ends, e.g. if the fiscal year ends on June 30, the month will be six.

sources.title: Calendarization - Overview, Formula, How it Works
sources.quote: Month # is the month when the company’s financial year ends

q: In comps analysis, what does the abbreviation LTM stand for?
explain: LTM, often used interchangeably with trailing twelve months (TTM), measures a metric over the most recent twelve-month period and is backward-looking.

sources.title: Last Twelve Months (LTM) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: LTM stands for “Last Twelve Months” and measures the performance of a metric, most often revenue, as of the trailing twelve-month period.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples - Using LTM vs NTM Multiples in Valuation
sources.quote: LTM stands for Last Twelve Months and TTM stands for Trailing Twelve Months , which is basically the historic or backward-looking multiple.

q: LTM equals the last fiscal year figure plus the recent year-to-date figure minus what?
explain: You add the stub period after the fiscal year-end and subtract the matching period from the prior year, so the total still covers twelve months.
hook: Add this year's stub, drop last year's matching stub.

sources.title: Last Twelve Months (LTM) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Last Twelve Months (LTM) = Last Fiscal Year Financial Data + Recent Year-to-Date Data – Prior YTD Data

sources.title: LTM vs. NTM Multiples | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Last Twelve Months (LTM) = Latest Fiscal Year Financial Data + Recent Year-to-Date Data – Prior YTD Data

q: What is the step of adding the period after the fiscal year-end and subtracting the matching prior period called in an LTM calculation?
explain: The stub periods added and subtracted must match in timing covered so the LTM figure spans exactly twelve months.

sources.title: Last Twelve Months (LTM) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The process of adding the period beyond the fiscal year ending date (and subtracting the matching period) is called the “stub period” adjustment.

sources.title: LTM vs. NTM Multiples | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The process of adding the period past the latest fiscal year and subtracting the matching period is referred to as the “stub period” adjustment.

q: For a U.S. public company, which SEC filing provides the year-to-date figures used in an LTM calculation?
explain: The latest annual data come from the 10-K, while the current and prior YTD figures come from the quarterly 10-Q filings.

sources.title: LTM vs. NTM Multiples | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The latest annual filing data can be found in its 10-K filings if the company is publicly traded. In contrast, the most recent year-to-date (YTD) and corresponding YTD data to deduct are recorded in the 10-Q filings.

sources.title: Last Twelve Months (LTM) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: If the company is publicly traded, the latest annual filing data can be found in its 10-K filings, whereas the most recent YTD and corresponding YTD financial metrics to deduct can be found in the 10-Q filings.

q: What does NTM stand for when describing forward valuation multiples?
explain: NTM multiples are formulated from projected figures, whereas LTM multiples are backward-looking and based on historical performance.

sources.title: LTM vs. NTM Multiples | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Last Twelve Months (LTM) and Next Twelve Months (NTM) are standard forms in which valuation multiples are presented in trading and transaction comps analyses. While LTM multiples are backward-looking and based on historical performance, NTM multiples are formulated from projected figures.

sources.title: Forward Multiple | Formula + Calculator - Wall Street Prep
sources.quote: Moreover, forward multiples are commonly based on a company’s estimated next twelve months (NTM) performance, but can be extended even further out.

q: Why is the median often preferred over the mean when summarizing a comps peer group's multiples?
wrong: It always produces a higher value
explain: Using the median removes the distortion caused by outliers; Macabacus calls it generally the most meaningful summary metric for that reason.
hook: Median = the middle, unbothered by extremes.

sources.title: Comparable Company Analysis | Trading Comps Tutorial
sources.quote: Median → Using the median removes the distortion caused by outliers, which increases in tandem with the number of comparable companies included.

sources.title: Comparable Companies Analysis - Trading Comps Examples | Macabacus
sources.quote: The median is generally the most meaningful metric, because it naturally screens outliers.

q: Which valuation multiple is the most commonly used in practice, especially in M&A?
explain: EV/EBITDA is the most used enterprise value multiple, with EBITDA serving as a proxy for cash flow available to the firm.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples Primer | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: In practice, the EV/EBITDA multiple is the most commonly used, followed by EV/EBIT, especially in the context of M&A.

sources.title: Types of Valuation Multiples – Equity & Enterprise Value Multiples
sources.quote: EV/EBITDA – EBITDA can be used as a substitute of free cash flows; is the most used enterprise value multiple; computed as Enterprise Value / Earnings before Interest, Tax, Depreciation & Amortization

q: Enterprise value multiples allow comparison of firms regardless of what, unlike equity value multiples?
explain: Enterprise value represents all capital providers, so EV multiples are capital structure neutral; equity value multiples such as P/E are influenced by leverage.
hook: EV sees debt and equity alike.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Enterprise vs Equity, P/E, EBITDA, EBIT, Sales | Macabacus
sources.quote: Enterprise value multiples are better than equity value multiples because the former allow for direct comparison of different firms, regardless of capital structure.

sources.title: Comparable Company Analysis | Trading Comps Tutorial
sources.quote: the most commonly used multiples in the industry are based on enterprise value, as such multiples are independent of the capital structure and focus on the core operations of the company.

q: Expressed in aggregate terms, the P/E multiple equals equity value divided by what?
explain: P/E is an equity value multiple, so its denominator must be a metric belonging to shareholders: net income (or EPS on a per-share basis).

sources.title: Valuation Multiples Primer | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: P/E Ratio = Equity Value ÷ Net Income

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Enterprise vs Equity, P/E, EBITDA, EBIT, Sales | Macabacus
sources.quote: Note that the P/E multiple equals the ratio of equity value to net Income, in which the numerator and denominator are both are divided by the number of fully diluted shares.

q: EV/Revenue is an enterprise value multiple; which revenue-based multiple is its equity value counterpart?
explain: Price-to-sales divides market capitalization by sales, so it values equity only; EV/Revenue values the firm for all stakeholders.

sources.title: Revenue Multiple | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Price-to-Sales (P/S) = Market Capitalization ÷ Sales

sources.title: Revenue Multiple | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Price-to-Sales → Equity Value Multiple

q: Which multiple is generally used to value unprofitable companies when EBITDA or EBIT is negative?
explain: When earnings are negative, earnings-based multiples become meaningless, so EV/Revenue is often the only meaningful option, common for early-stage, high-growth companies.

sources.title: EV/Revenue Multiple | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Generally, the EV/Revenue multiple is used for unprofitable companies with negative profit margins, or limited profitability, rendering other valuation multiples to be meaningless.

sources.title: Valuation Multiples: Enterprise vs Equity, P/E, EBITDA, EBIT, Sales | Macabacus
sources.quote: When a company has negative EBITDA, the EV/EBITDA and EV/EBIT multiples will not be material. In such cases, EV/Sales may be the most appropriate multiple to use.

q: In the basic formula, annual recurring revenue (ARR) equals monthly recurring revenue (MRR) multiplied by what number?
explain: ARR is conceptually the annualized MRR of a subscription business, so MRR is multiplied by twelve months.

sources.title: Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) = Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) × 12 Months

sources.title: Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) - Calculation and Examples
sources.quote: Annual Recurring Revenue (ARR) = Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) × 12

q: The ARR multiple divides which value measure by annual recurring revenue?
explain: The ARR multiple (EV/ARR) shows how much investors pay for each dollar of recurring revenue; enterprise value, not market cap, is used because it represents the total acquisition cost.

sources.title: ARR Multiple: Definition, Formula, and Examples | CFI
sources.quote: The ARR multiple is enterprise value divided by annual recurring revenue (ARR). It shows how much investors pay for each dollar of recurring revenue.

sources.title: ARR Multiple: Definition, Formula, and Examples | CFI
sources.quote: Use enterprise value (not market cap) because it represents the total acquisition cost.

q: Under the Rule of 40, a SaaS company's revenue growth rate plus profit margin should be at least what percentage?
explain: The Rule of 40 is a rule-of-thumb benchmark for balancing growth against profitability in SaaS companies.

sources.title: The SaaS Rule of 40 Explained | CFI
sources.quote: The Rule of 40 says that the sum of the revenue growth rate and the profit margin should be 40% or higher.

sources.title: The Rule of 40 (Brad Feld) | SaaS Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The Rule of 40 states that if an SaaS company’s revenue growth rate is added to its profit margin, the combined value should exceed 40%.

q: Which profit margin is most commonly used in the Rule of 40 calculation?
explain: EBITDA margin is the most common choice because most growth-stage companies are unprofitable or barely profitable on GAAP metrics such as EBIT.

sources.title: The Rule of 40 (Brad Feld) | SaaS Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: As for the profit margin, the most common metric used is the EBITDA margin in the corresponding period.

sources.title: The SaaS Rule of 40 Explained | CFI
sources.quote: Additionally, there are different profit margin calculations, with EBITDA margin being the most common approach.

q: For the growth component of the Rule of 40, analysts typically favor growth in which type of revenue?
explain: The growth rate typically refers to MRR or ARR growth rather than gross or net revenue, since GAAP metrics often fail to capture SaaS performance.

sources.title: The Rule of 40 (Brad Feld) | SaaS Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: The revenue growth rate, rather than referring to the gross or net revenue of a company, typically refers to the monthly recurring revenue ( MRR ) or annual recurring revenue ( ARR ).

sources.title: The SaaS Rule of 40 Explained | CFI
sources.quote: There are different ways to calculate revenue growth, but most analysts favor using a recurring revenue stream.

q: What is the Rule of 40 score of a SaaS company with 100% revenue growth and a negative 60% profit margin?
explain: 100% + (-60%) = 40%, which technically meets the rule; CFI uses this case to show the Rule of 40 is only a benchmark and needs further analysis.

sources.title: The SaaS Rule of 40 Explained | CFI
sources.quote: Of course, the above scenarios are likely more preferable compared to a company with a 100% revenue growth rate but a negative 60% profit margin, which would technically meet the Rule of 40 (100% + -60%).

sources.title: The Rule of 40 (Brad Feld) | SaaS Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: Rule of 40 (%) = Recurring Revenue Growth Rate (%) + EBITDA Margin (%)

q: Compared with trading comps, what timing weakness do precedent transactions have?
wrong: They rely only on projected figures
explain: Precedent multiples reflect past deals and can become stale as markets move, whereas comps reflect current public market prices.

sources.title: Precedent Transaction Analysis - Definition, Steps
sources.quote: Timing (precedents quickly become old– comps are current)

sources.title: Valuation Methods - Three Main Approaches to Value a Business
sources.quote: They are useful for M&A transactions but can easily become stale and no longer reflect the current market as time passes.

q: In the industry-specific multiple EV/EBITDAR, what cost does the 'R' add back to EBITDA?
explain: EV/EBITDAR adds back rental costs and is most used in the hotel and transportation sectors.
hook: R for Rent: airlines and hotels lease a lot.

sources.title: Types of Valuation Multiples – Equity & Enterprise Value Multiples
sources.quote: EV/EBITDAR – most used in industries in the hotel and transport sectors; computed as the proportion of Enterprise Value to Earnings before Interest, Tax, Depreciation & Amortization, and Rental Costs

sources.title: Valuation Multiples Primer | Formula + Calculator
sources.quote: For example, EV/EBITDAR is frequently seen in the transportation industry (i.e. rental costs are added back to EBITDA), while EV/(EBITDA – Capex ) is frequently used for industrials and other capital-intensive industries like manufacturing.

q: The justified EV/EBITDA multiple has an inverse relationship with which fundamental driver?
explain: Per CFA Institute, justified EV/EBITDA rises with expected FCFF growth and profitability and falls as the weighted average cost of capital rises.

sources.title: Market-Based Valuation: Price and Enterprise Value Multiples | CFA Institute
sources.quote: The fundamental drivers of EV/EBITDA are the expected growth rate in free cash flow to the firm, profitability, and the weighted average cost of capital. The justified EV/EBITDA based on fundamentals bears a positive relationship to the first two factors and an inverse relationship to the third.
